power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p ≥ 0.30", Text = "No treatmentby-timepoint interaction (p = 0.30 and 0.71) or carryover effect (p ≥ 0.30) was detected for either muscle."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

ethics_statements: The Northwestern University Institutional Review Board approved this study (STU00219535), and all participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06276634).
The event was reported to the IRB, and fall-risk language was added to the informed consent form and protocol.
The study was approved by the Northwestern University Institutional Review Board (STU00219535) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06276634) before enrollment began.
live_data_statements: Participants were assigned to receive both AIH and Sham AIH, in a random order, with a minimum 4-week washout period between blocks to reduce carryover effects.
The Northwestern University Institutional Review Board approved this study (STU00219535), and all participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06276634).
Participants were recruited from the neurology clinics of Northwestern Memorial Hospital and the Shirley Ryan AbilityLab Clinical Research Registry.

We administered AIH and Sham AIH using a Hypoxico HYP-123 hypoxic air generator (Hypoxico Inc., New York, NY), consistent with prior AIH studies in humans with neurological conditions. 10, 11, [15] [16] [17] Participants were seated and fitted with a non-rebreathing face mask connected to the generator via an inlet line.
Participants were unable to distinguish AIH from Sham based on the breathing experience.
Participants were secured in the dynamometer and instructed to push (plantarflexion) or pull (dorsiflexion) against the footplate for 3 s.
Walking speed was quantified using the T25FW, a component of the MS Functional Composite. 19 Participants were instructed to walk a clearly marked 25-foot course at maximum safe effort.
Participants were modeled as a random effect with an unstructured covariance matrix to account for the repeated-measures structure of the crossover design.

Twenty-five participants provided written informed consent and were randomized; 2 withdrew before completing both intervention blocks (1 due to commute issues, 1 due to scheduling conflicts) and were not included in any analyses.
Twenty-three participants completed both intervention blocks.
This session was terminated, and the participant completed the remaining sessions without any adverse events after physician review.

All participants completed follow-up MRI after both the AIH and Sham intervention blocks, and no new or enlarging T2/FLAIR lesions, gadolinium-enhancing lesions, or diffusion abnormalities were identified in any participant in either arm.

Of 23 participants, 20 completed Biodex assessments and 18 completed all six assessment visits; the remaining participants were unable to complete one or more assessments due to scheduling and clinical constraints.
All participants provided written informed consent before participation.
Twenty-five participants were enrolled, 2 discontinued (commute issues, n = 1; schedule conflict, n = 1), and 23 completed the study.
